name: Aleut

ancestors.notes: Descent per Glottolog classification of Aleut (aleu1260).

notes: Skeleton. Eskimo-Aleut (Aleut/Unangam) language of the Aleutian Islands written in the Bergsland practical Latin orthography (Bergsland 1994, 1997) — the dominant modern writing system for Aleut (a historical Cyrillic orthography, introduced by Russian Orthodox missionaries in the 19th century, is now a minority/heritage convention; Latin is the one used in current pedagogical and dictionary materials, so it is the one modelled here). Long vowels are doubled (aa ii uu); ng=[ŋ], d=[ð], g=[ɣ] with circumflexed x̂=[χ] and ĝ=[ʁ] for the uvular fricatives, and l̂=[ɬ] are mapped. The h-prefixed voiceless sonorants (hm hn hng hl hw hy) are mapped to voiceless counterparts. The voiceless palato-alveolar affricate ch=[tʃ] (Bergsland 1994, p. xvi orthography table; corroborated by the phoneme inventory in Taff et al. 2001, 'Phonetic Structures of Aleut', Journal of Phonetics 29(3), doi:10.1006/jpho.2001.0142) was missing from earlier versions of this table despite being a core native phoneme, not a loanword-only sound. Taff et al. 2001 also documents (p), (b), (d), (g), (f), v and (ɹ,ɾ) as consonants that occur only in loanwords in Aleut, spelled with their plain Latin letters; b, v, r, f and p are mapped on that basis for the loanword layer (Russian month/weekday/animal borrowings such as 'baraaska', 'Yanvaari', 'Subuuta' in the gold). Predictable stress is left unencoded. IMPORTANT — gold-vs-orthography finding: the NorthEuraLex `ale` (northeuralex gold, Dellert2020 source column) forms were checked directly against this spec's tokenizer. The Value column consistently spells the two uvular fricatives with a COMBINING ACUTE ACCENT (U+0301) over x and g — ⟨x́⟩, ⟨ǵ⟩ — rather than the circumflex ⟨x̂⟩/⟨ĝ⟩ that Bergsland's practical orthography (and this spec) writes; this affects 497 of 896 rows (55.5%) and is the largest single driver of the tokenizer's unmapped-character rate, measured directly against the northeuralex gold only (not the union-across-datasets figure the mechanical diagnostic reports). Rather than rewrite the gold or change the spec's canonical spelling, `x́` and `ǵ` are mapped as alternate spellings of the SAME already-sourced uvular phonemes (χ, ʁ). A further 4/896 rows (0.4%) carry a precomposed acute-accented ⟨í⟩ immediately after one of these forms (e.g. 'chiǵilǵí-x́'), which on inspection is not a distinct phoneme but reads as a stress mark on /i/ in this transcription; it is mapped to plain i (stress already left unencoded elsewhere in this spec) rather than modelled as a new phonological contrast — this rests on a distributional observation, not a citation. The gold also shows a systematic vowel-quality shift not attested in Aleut phonology under Bergsland's analysis (unstressed i to [e], u to [y]/[o], a to [ɛ]/[ɑ] depending on the word, doubled aa to [ɛː] rather than [aː]); this is a narrow phonetic transcription of a specific recorded pronunciation (or a distinct source dialect's realization), not the practical orthography Aleut is written in, and modelling it as if it were the spelling would misdescribe the language, so it is documented as a gold transcription-convention mismatch rather than chased with orthography-violating rules. Measured directly (vowel-skeleton comparison between hypothesis and gold on every non-exact row), this shift alone touches 772 of the 813 non-exact rows (94.9% of all residual errors, 86.2% of the full 896-row gold) — e.g. `adi-x́` -> `aðiχ` against gold `adeχ`, `agalu-x́` -> `aɣaluχ` against gold `agaloχ` — and accounts for most of the remaining 0.2634 PER floor. Separately, the reviewer also noticed that this spec's blanket g->ɣ and d->ð rules look wrong in some cluster contexts, where the gold keeps plain [g]/[d]: `kamg-` gives gold `kamg` (not `kamɣ`), and `qiiliqda-x́` gives gold `qeːleqdɑχ` (keeping plain `d`). That looks like unmodelled positional/cluster allophony (g/d perhaps spirantizing only intervocalically or word-medially, not after another consonant), is PRE-EXISTING (predates this PR, not introduced by it), and is left as an open question for a future spec revision rather than fixed here without a source for the conditioning environment. Hyphens in the gold mark a stem/suffix citation-form boundary and are already stripped as punctuation by the engine. There are no homographs in the northeuralex gold for `ale` (896 distinct spellings, 896 distinct transcriptions). This spec keeps the real Bergsland Latin orthography and stays at `skeleton`.
